The partial-write reproduction is a deliberately paused, single-process sequential write on real local disk, not a genuine two-process race — it reproduces the shape of the failure (a listing taken mid-write sees an inconsistent state) rather than claiming to model exact multi-writer timing.

items.item: The listing-cost measurement is this sandbox's own local disk, not S3's documented LIST latency or its per-prefix request-rate limits (both already covered with real AWS numbers in the previous topic) — only the qualitative shape (cost grows with file count) is claimed here.

items.item: Hive's own 'dirty reads' wording in its Transactions wiki describes in-progress streaming writes within a single partition; this topic draws an explicit, not implicit, connection to the cross-partition case it reproduces, since both share the same root cause (no atomic commit boundary) without claiming they are identical scenarios.

at.step: Reveal: this is Hive's own documented reason for adding ACID

items.item: Hive 0.13 is cited as a historical pre/post marker, not as the final word on Hive's current ACID capabilities — Hive continued adding transactional features afterward; this topic frames the pre-ACID gap as what motivated other table formats (Iceberg, Delta), not as Hive being permanently unfixed.

at.step: Predict: can a write to two partitions commit as one atomic unit?

items.item: The local-filesystem stand-in for object storage is disclosed explicitly in examples.py's own docstring: this sandbox has no real multi-petabyte S3 bucket, but the filesystem-listing mechanics demonstrated (a listing reflecting only currently-existing files, cost growing with file count) are the same mechanics a real object-store LIST call has.

Partition-value validation (or its absence) and atomic multi-partition commits are two separate failure modes with two separate root causes in Hive's design — the first is a writer-trust problem (no check against the row), the second is a transaction-boundary problem (no commit wrapping multiple files) — this topic keeps them distinct rather than conflating them as one issue.

items.item: The §6.3.3 Hudi material is entirely skipped per CHAPTER.md's own plan; this topic names only Hive, Iceberg and Delta, never Hudi, consistent with that chapter-wide decision.

MSCK REPAIR TABLE's cost scaling with partition count (Cloudera's own documented behavior) is distinct from this topic's own measured os.scandir() curve (a raw filesystem listing call) — the topic draws the parallel explicitly (both get slower as the thing being listed grows) without claiming they are the same operation.
